items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

ctx.x: No, no, no, no. Larry King. He had Eric Clapton on. And he was playing guitar, and I think except the way I heard him and his writings with the guitar, mainly today, well a point I want to make is a lot of today’s music is being written by guitar players. You can’t — with the guitar you miss the beauty of a Tchaikovsky, like [scats], you know the third in the bass. The seventh and the bass. With a guitar you always have the tonic in the bass. And I think that’s missing a little bit in the younger writers today.…

It’s interesting you mention that, because if you look at — recently I was looking at some of the music from “West Side Story,” and “One Hand One Heart.” And that’s what Bernstein did. He had very simple chords, but he would put the third in the bass, and it changed the whole thing, it gave it a real beautiful effect.

Well if you took Tchaikovsky and put the melody in the bass line, you’ve practically got a composition and a score like this you know. But with today’s writers, everything’s going like this. But there’s something about that contrary motion and the movement of the bass, it’s great. But I learned that from breaking those scores down, you know, and I thought wow, what a sound, that’s great, that’s how they do that, huh? And I’d hunt, and wait a minute now, have an F chord and there would be an A in the bass, and I’d…
